Slack vs WhatsApp vs Discord vs Circle: Which Platform Should a B2B Community Use?

Slack, WhatsApp, Discord or Circle for a B2B community? Compare cost, limits, data ownership, India vs US habits and which platforms Google and AI search can read.

By Anupam Varshney, Founder, Octaloop

Short answer: Choose the platform your members already open every day. That means WhatsApp for an India-first, mobile-first community; Slack for US professionals who spend their workday in it; Discord for developer and technical communities that need free scale; and Circle when you want a branded, paid or course-led community that you control. None of the three chat apps (Slack, WhatsApp or Discord) can be read by Google or AI search engines. If you want your community's knowledge to bring you discovery, add a public, indexable layer such as public Circle spaces, a Discourse forum or recap pages on your own site.

In 2016 I started an 8-person Bitcoin meetup in Delhi. It grew into India Blockchain Tour and the Metamorphosis summit, with more than 13,000 attendees across editions. In that time I have watched communities live on almost every tool, and I have seen good communities die on the wrong one. The platform won't make a community, but the wrong one can quietly break it. Members stop opening it, history disappears, or you find you can't take your own members with you when you leave.

In this guide I compare the four platforms B2B founders ask me about most, using each vendor's own pricing and help pages (checked 27 October 2026) and the newest independent data I could find.

What do community professionals actually use in 2026?

There is no single winner. The 2026 CMX Community Industry Report (published July 2026, powered by Bevy) surveyed 305 community professionals in May and June 2026. Most were in the US (56.7%) and 7.6% were in India. Among respondents who named a primary forum or community platform (n=156), the spread was:

Primary community platform (CMX 2026) Share of respondents
Slack 19.9%
WhatsApp 16.7%
Discord 12.8%
Discourse 12.2%
Circle 12.2%
Facebook group 8.3%
Khoros 7.7%
Salesforce 7.7%
LinkedIn group 7.7%
Higher Logic Vanilla 5.8%

Source: CMX, 2026 Community Industry Report, July 2026.

CMX says "platform fragmentation is the norm" and that chat-first tools (Slack, WhatsApp, Discord) now rival purpose-built community platforms. Its conclusion matches what I have seen: "Meeting members where they already are matters more than any single 'right' tool."

So the useful question is not "which tool is best?" but "which tool fits my members, budget and goals?"

How do Slack, WhatsApp, Discord and Circle compare?

Here is the side-by-side view. Prices and limits come from each vendor's official pages, checked on 27 October 2026.

When should a B2B community choose Slack?

Choose Slack when your members are professionals who already have Slack open all day for work. That is common with US SaaS operators, revenue leaders, product managers and developers at funded startups. A community in Slack sits next to their work, so it gets checked.

The catch is cost and memory:

  • The free plan forgets. According to Slack's help centre, free workspaces can view and search only the last 90 days of messages and files, and anything older than one year is permanently deleted. For a community, that means your best answers disappear.
  • Paid plans scale with members. Slack Pro is $8.75 per user per month on monthly billing (Slack pricing, checked 27 October 2026). Slack's fair billing policy charges only for members who are active, but the cost still rises with your community. As a simple illustration, 300 active members on Pro works out to $2,625 a month.
  • Free-plan features are thin for communities. Huddles and Slack Connect are 1:1 only on Free, and you can only control who posts in #general on Free and Pro.

Verdict: Slack is great for a small, high-value community of 50–500 professionals (customer advisory groups, peer groups for founders or CROs, partner communities), especially in the US. It is a poor long-term home for a large free community whose knowledge you want to keep.

When is WhatsApp the right choice for a professional community?

In India, WhatsApp is the default. Meta has said WhatsApp has more than 500 million users in India (TechCrunch, 31 December 2024). Founders, CXOs, sales leaders and event attendees in India answer WhatsApp faster than email, so a WhatsApp community gets the highest open rates of anything on this list for an India-first audience.

The US is different. Pew Research Center's 2026 social media fact sheet (published 19 October 2026, based on 5,511 US adults surveyed January–June 2026) found that 33% of US adults use WhatsApp. Usage is higher among college graduates (43%), urban adults (44%), Hispanic adults (56%) and Asian adults (51%). So WhatsApp can work for a US professional audience, but it is not the default the way it is in India.

What to know before you commit:

  • Size limits. A WhatsApp group holds up to 1,024 members (WhatsApp Help Center). A WhatsApp Community can link up to 100 groups and hold up to 2,000 members including the announcement group (WhatsApp Help Center). WhatsApp also notes you can't create a Community from the WhatsApp Business app.
  • Announcement groups are the killer feature. Every Community gets an announcement group where only admins post to everyone. For event organisers, that is the cleanest way to send updates without burying them in chat.
  • History is weak. New members don't see earlier conversations unless an admin or member chooses to send them between 25 and 100 recent messages (WhatsApp blog, 19 February 2026). Search runs on each member's phone, so nothing builds into a shared knowledge base.
  • No owner export. Individual members can export a chat from their phone, but there is no admin dashboard, analytics or member export.

Verdict: WhatsApp is the best activation and announcements channel for India-first communities, events and city chapters. It is the worst place to store knowledge. If your WhatsApp group has gone quiet, my guide to reviving a dead Slack or WhatsApp community has a 30-day plan.

When does Discord make sense for B2B?

Discord is no longer only for gamers. The company reports more than 200 million monthly active users (Discord newsroom). In India, Discord had 11 million monthly active mobile users in August 2025, making it the app's third-largest market by mobile MAU, according to Sensor Tower data reported by BusinessLine (16 September 2025). The same article describes startups using Discord for customer support, feedback and community discussion, and adoption spreading from 18–24-year-olds to 25–34-year-olds.

Discord's strengths are scale and cost. A server can hold up to 25 million members with 500 channels and 250 roles, and the core product is free (Discord server caps, updated 2 March 2026). Roles and permissions are far richer than WhatsApp's, and voice channels and Stage events make live sessions easy.

The downsides for B2B:

  • Learning curve. A user quoted in the BusinessLine piece called the UX "a very steep learning curve." Non-technical buyers such as marketers, finance teams and executives often don't have Discord installed.
  • Notifications thin out at scale. In servers above 2,500 members, Discord stops sending mobile push notifications for every message, and the offline member list is hidden once a server passes 1,000 members.
  • Not public. Discord's robots.txt blocks crawlers from /channels/, where messages live, so your best technical answers don't reach Google or AI search. Server Discovery inside Discord requires at least 1,000 members and a server that is at least 8 weeks old (Discord support).

Verdict: Discord is the right default for developer tools, APIs, open source, AI products and technical communities that expect thousands of free members. For a community of non-technical B2B buyers, it is usually the wrong choice.

When should you pay for Circle?

Circle is a purpose-built community platform. You pay for it, and in return you get a branded home that you control. Pricing on circle.so/pricing (checked 27 October 2026, annual billing) is $89/month for Professional, $199/month for Business and $419/month for Scale, with Circle Plus at custom pricing. Every plan allows unlimited members. Transaction fees on paid memberships range from 2% to 0.5% depending on the plan.

What you get that chat apps don't:

  • Structure. Spaces for discussions, events, courses and member directories, plus a weekly email digest that brings back members who don't open the app.
  • Ownership. Your own domain, bulk member import/export, and billing for paid memberships.
  • Discoverability. Circle lets you set a community to public and turn on "Let search engines index your site", with titles, meta descriptions and a sitemap (Circle Knowledge Base). None of the three chat apps can do this.

The trade-off is that Circle is another app or tab your members must remember to open. Professional also caps you at 3 admins and 20 spaces, and branded mobile apps are only on Circle Plus.

Verdict: Pay for Circle when the community is the product (paid membership, cohort course, certification) or when it is a strategic customer community you want to own and make discoverable. Don't pay for it to host a 40-person peer group that would be happier in WhatsApp or Slack.

What about Discourse, Skool and LinkedIn groups?

Three alternatives come up often:

  • Discourse is an open-source forum used by 12.2% of CMX respondents. Its hosted plans start free (2 staff seats, 10 categories) and go up to $100/month for Pro and $500/month for Business, or you can self-host at no licence cost (Discourse pricing, checked 27 October 2026). Public Discourse topics are served to search engine crawlers as server-rendered HTML with sitemaps (Discourse Meta). That makes it the strongest choice when you want community answers to rank.
  • Skool combines community and courses for creators. Hobby is $9/month and Pro is $99/month (Skool pricing). Transaction fees are 10% + 30¢ on Hobby and 2.9% + 30¢ on Pro for prices up to $899 (Skool Help Center, updated 29 September 2026). It is built for paid creator communities, not B2B customer communities.
  • LinkedIn groups were the primary platform for 7.7% of CMX respondents. They are easy to join but hard to keep active. For most B2B founders, your personal LinkedIn feed reaches more people than a group, as I explain in my guide to founder-led marketing on LinkedIn.

Why does it matter whether your community is public or private for AI search?

This is the angle most platform comparisons miss, and it matters more every month.

AI search engines lean heavily on community content. A Peec AI study of 30 million sources, reported by Search Engine Land (31 March 2026), found Reddit was the most-cited domain across ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, Gemini, Perplexity and AI Overviews, followed by YouTube and LinkedIn. For B2B queries, Perplexity leaned on Reddit, LinkedIn and G2. Ahrefs' UGC citation tracker shows Reddit cited in 10.13% of Google AI Overview responses it tracked on 25 October 2026, based on 9.9 million responses.

Engines can only cite what they can read. Slack workspaces, WhatsApp groups and Discord servers are closed to crawlers. Every brilliant answer your members give there is invisible to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google. CMX flags this as an emerging issue for the first time in 2026: most community teams "can't yet track whether their content shows up in AI answers", and the report says AI search visibility "may become a discoverability play."

Public and indexable beats private when:

  • Members ask the same product, how-to or comparison questions again and again. Those answers are exactly what buyers type into AI search.
  • You sell to people who research in ChatGPT or Perplexity before talking to sales.
  • Your community is a reason to buy (for example, a strong user community for a developer tool).

Private beats public when:

  • Members share numbers, salaries, deals or customer names (peer groups, CXO circles).
  • Trust and candour are the product.
  • The community is mainly for event logistics and announcements.

The hybrid most B2B teams should run: keep conversation in the chat app members already use, and publish the best of it in a public, indexable place. That could be public Circle spaces, a Discourse forum, or simply FAQ and recap pages on your own site. Remove names and get permission where you need it. If you want the full playbook on getting cited, read how to get your SaaS mentioned in ChatGPT, Perplexity and AI Overviews.

How do you pick the right platform for your community?

Answer these five questions in order:

  1. Where do your members already spend their day? India-first founders and attendees → WhatsApp. US professionals → Slack. Developers → Discord. If your members are spread out, start where the most active 20% live.
  2. How big will it get in 12 months? Under 1,000 → any of them. Over 2,000 → not WhatsApp alone. Thousands of free members → Discord, Circle or Discourse rather than paid Slack.
  3. Do you need to keep knowledge? If yes, avoid Slack Free and WhatsApp as your only home.
  4. Do you want discovery from Google and AI search? If yes, you need a public layer (Circle public spaces, Discourse or your own site).
  5. Will members pay? If yes, Circle or Skool handle billing; chat apps don't.

If you are still at the meetup stage, start in person first. My guide to organising meetups that grow into a community shows how a small room turns into a network. Pick the online platform after you know who keeps showing up.

What should you check before migrating your community?

Most communities lose members when they migrate. Use this checklist to keep the loss small:

  • Export everything you can first. On Slack Free or Pro, export public channels (Free only keeps file links from the last 90 days). Download member lists, emails and event attendee data from every source.
  • Write down why you are moving. Members will ask. "We lose our history every 90 days" or "we've hit WhatsApp's 1,024-member cap" are reasons people accept.
  • Recruit 10–20 champions first. Get your most active members into the new space before the announcement so it isn't empty on day one.
  • Seed the new space. Recreate the top 10–20 threads or FAQs from the old platform so newcomers find value immediately.
  • Announce three times, in three places. Old platform, email and LinkedIn, over two to three weeks.
  • Set a clear end date for the old space, and switch it to announcements-only rather than deleting it straight away.
  • Run a launch moment. An AMA, a live session or a meetup in the first week gives people a reason to show up.
  • Keep the old channel as a pointer. Pin a message with the new link for at least three months.
  • Measure for 30 days. Track weekly active members and posts per week against the old platform. If activity drops, use the community revival plan.

FAQ

Is Slack or Discord better for a B2B community?

Slack is usually better for non-technical B2B professionals because many already use it at work, especially in the US. Discord is better for developer and technical communities that expect thousands of free members, since it is free and supports up to 25 million members per server. Slack's free plan only shows the last 90 days of messages, and Pro costs $8.75 per active user per month on monthly billing.

Is WhatsApp good for a professional community?

Yes, especially in India, where Meta reports more than 500 million WhatsApp users. WhatsApp gets fast responses and its Communities feature has an announcement group for admin updates. Its limits are 1,024 members per group and 2,000 per community, no admin analytics or export, and new members only see past messages if someone sends them up to 100 recent ones.

How much does Circle cost in 2026?

On Circle's pricing page (checked 27 October 2026), annual billing costs $89/month for Professional, $199/month for Business and $419/month for Scale, with Circle Plus at custom pricing. All plans include unlimited members, and a 14-day free trial is available. Transaction fees on paid memberships range from 2% to 0.5% depending on the plan.

Can Google or ChatGPT read my Slack, Discord or WhatsApp community?

No. Slack workspaces and WhatsApp groups are private, WhatsApp messages are end-to-end encrypted, and Discord blocks crawlers from its /channels/ pages. To make community knowledge citable in AI search, publish it in a public, indexable place such as public Circle spaces, a Discourse forum or FAQ pages on your own website.

What is the member limit for WhatsApp groups and communities?

A WhatsApp group can have up to 1,024 members. A WhatsApp Community can link up to 100 groups and hold up to 2,000 members including the announcement group, according to WhatsApp's Help Center. You can't create a Community from the WhatsApp Business app.

Should a B2B community run on more than one platform?

Often, yes. The 2026 CMX Community Industry Report found that platform fragmentation is the norm. A common setup is a chat app for daily conversation (WhatsApp in India, Slack in the US, Discord for developers) plus a public layer such as Circle, Discourse or your own website for knowledge that should be searchable and citable by AI engines.
